common_name: Chef's Choice Orange Tomato (AAS-Winning Orange Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Chef's Choice Orange is a vigorous indeterminate beefsteak tomato bred from the heirloom Amana Orange with improved disease resistance, and needs sturdy staking or caging for the large fruit.

directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine well before it needs the support. Chef's Choice Orange is an AAS National Winner bred from the beloved heirloom Amana Orange, keeping its rich, sweet, low-acid flavor and bright orange beefsteak-size fruit while adding the disease resistance and productivity of a modern hybrid. Fruits regularly reach a pound or more, with a meaty, low-seed interior well suited to slicing, and the vivid orange color makes a striking addition to a mixed tomato platter or salad. Prune suckers lightly on the lower third of the plant to improve airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture even, since large-fruited beefsteaks are more prone to blossom-end rot and cracking under fluctuating moisture.
sources: All-America Selections — Chef's Choice Orange Tomato winner announcement

common_name: Terenzo Tomato (AAS-Winning Trailing Tumbler Cherry Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Terenzo is a compact, self-branching trailing cherry tomato bred specifically for hanging baskets and containers, needing no staking or pruning.

directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into a hanging basket, window box, or large container filled with fertile, well-drained potting mix in full sun. Terenzo is an AAS-winning cherry tomato bred as a true tumbler type — a compact, mounding, self-branching plant that spills gracefully over the edge of a container rather than climbing, producing a heavy, non-stop crop of small, sweet red cherry tomatoes without any staking, caging, or pruning. Its small scale and container-ready habit make it one of the easiest tomatoes for a patio, balcony, or small-space garden with no in-ground bed at all. Water container plantings regularly, since pots dry out faster than garden soil, and feed every couple of weeks through the season to sustain the heavy, continuous fruit set.

common_name: Valentine Tomato (AAS-Winning Sweet Red Grape Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Valentine is a vigorous indeterminate grape tomato bred for very early, heavy, and sustained fruit set, and needs sturdy staking or caging for the long fruiting vine.

directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, then stake or cage the vigorous vine well before it needs support. Valentine is an AAS National Winner producing deep red, oblong grape tomatoes with an exceptionally sweet, well-balanced flavor and a notably early, heavy first flush of fruit compared to most grape tomatoes, extending the harvest window at both ends of the season. The disease-resistant vine is highly productive over a long season and holds up well to the heat and humidity of a full Gulf South summer. Harvest fruit as it fully colors for the best sweetness, and pick regularly to keep new clusters setting; the crack-resistant skin makes fruit more forgiving of uneven watering than many cherry and grape types.

common_name: Saladmore Bush Cucumber (AAS-Winning Compact Slicing Cucumber)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Saladmore Bush is a compact, semi-bush slicing cucumber (about 24 inches of spread) bred for strong disease resistance and small-space growing.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Saladmore Bush is an AAS-winning slicing cucumber bred for a genuinely compact semi-bush habit that still delivers a full-size harvest of straight, dark-green, 8-inch slicing cucumbers with crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor, on a plant that fits easily into small beds and large pots where a standard vining slicer would sprawl. It also carries strong resistance to several common cucumber diseases, giving it good vigor through a long summer season in humid climates. Keep soil evenly moist, especially as fruit is sizing, to avoid bitterness and misshapen cucumbers, and harvest regularly once fruiting begins to keep the plant productive.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Cayennetta is a compact cayenne-type pepper bred with sturdy branches that hold the fruit upright without staking, and with milder heat than a traditional cayenne.

directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cayennetta is an AAS-winning cayenne-type pepper bred for a compact, sturdy, well-branched plant that holds its heavy load of slender, upward-pointing red fruit without staking, unlike tall traditional cayenne varieties that tend to flop under the fruit's weight. The heat is noticeably milder than classic cayenne — moderate rather than fiery — making it more versatile for cooks who want cayenne flavor and color without maximum heat. Fruits can be picked green or left to ripen to full red for the best flavor and heat development, and the tidy plant size suits containers as well as garden beds. Harvest continuously to keep the plant setting new fruit through the season.

common_name: Katarina Cabbage (AAS-Winning Early Compact Mini Cabbage)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for a fall crop; Katarina is a very early, small-headed cabbage bred for close spacing in containers and small beds, forming a solid head faster than most cabbage varieties.

directions: Start transplants and set out in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Katarina is an AAS-winning cabbage bred for very early maturity and a small, tidy head about 4 inches across, forming a solid, sweet, light-green head faster than nearly any other garden cabbage — a useful trait for squeezing a crop into a short spring or fall window, or for a large container where a full-size storage cabbage would be impractical. Its small stature and rapid maturity also make it a good choice for succession planting through a cool season. Harvest as soon as heads feel firm and dense, since even fast-maturing types can split if left too long once mature. Watch for cabbage worms and aphids, common pests on all brassicas in the Gulf South.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Surefire is a determinate tomato bred by Texas A&M AgriLife specifically to keep setting fruit through the high nighttime temperatures that shut down bloom-to-fruit set in most tomato varieties across the Gulf South and Deep South summer.

directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Surefire is a Texas A&M AgriLife release and Texas Superstar-designated tomato bred specifically to hold fruit set through the punishing high nighttime heat of a Central and South Texas summer, when most tomato varieties stop setting fruit almost entirely — a trait directly useful across the wider Gulf South wherever midsummer heat causes the familiar tomato slump between the spring and fall crops. The compact, determinate plant produces a concentrated, heavy crop of medium-size, firm, flavorful red fruit over a shorter, more manageable staking and pruning window than a sprawling indeterminate vine. Because it is bred to keep fruiting through heat rather than avoid it, it is a good choice to extend the harvest into the hottest stretch of a zone 9 summer where other varieties stall.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Ramapo is a vigorous indeterminate slicing tomato bred at Rutgers University in 1968 and revived by popular demand decades later specifically for old-fashioned, full-bodied tomato flavor.

directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vine. Ramapo was bred at the Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station in 1968 and quickly became beloved throughout the New Jersey area for its rich, well-balanced, old-fashioned tomato flavor, but it fell out of commercial availability for decades until gardener demand led Rutgers to bring seed back into production through its 'Rediscover the Jersey Tomato' program. It combines much of the deep, sweet-tart flavor complexity associated with heirloom tomatoes with the disease resistance and reliability of a modern hybrid, producing medium-to-large red slicing fruit over a long summer season. Prune suckers lightly on the lower part of the plant for better airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture consistent, which reduces cracking and blossom-end rot on the larger fruit.

common_name: Dolce Fresca Basil (AAS-Winning Compact Genovese Basil)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Dolce Fresca is a compact, slow-to-bolt Genovese-type basil bred to hold a tidy, dense mounded shape through the season in beds or containers.

directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a container on a sunny patio. Dolce Fresca is an AAS-winning Genovese-type basil bred for a naturally compact, dense, dome-shaped habit and slower bolting than standard Genovese basil, so it holds its productive shape and classic sweet, clove-and-anise basil flavor for a longer stretch of the season without becoming leggy or rushing to flower. Its tidy size makes it especially well suited to containers, window boxes, and small kitchen gardens where a full-size Genovese plant would sprawl. Pinch growing tips regularly and remove any flower spikes as they form to keep the plant bushy and delay bolting further; harvest leaves anytime once the plant is established, picking in the morning for the best flavor.
sources: All-America Selections — Dolce Fresca Basil winner announcement

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun; Suziblue is a University of Georgia southern highbush release bred for reliable production in the low-chill Gulf South, and benefits from planting alongside a second southern highbush variety for improved pollination and fruit size.

directions: Plant in strongly acidic, well-drained soil generously amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Suziblue is a University of Georgia-bred southern highbush blueberry selected for a relatively low chilling requirement suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South, ripening its crop of large, firm, light-blue berries with good flavor early in the blueberry season, ahead of many other southern highbush varieties. Like all blueberries it needs consistently acidic soil and will struggle or fail in neutral to alkaline ground; test soil pH before planting and amend with elemental sulfur if needed. Plant it with a second, compatible southern highbush cultivar nearby to improve pollination, berry size, and total yield, since cross-pollination generally outperforms a single variety planted alone. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, and water regularly during dry spells and through fruit development.
